Local-first web search is a privacy primitive

By Alec Feeman — January 2026

Most agentic harnesses today route their search queries through a vendor-controlled endpoint. The user types a question, the model decides to search, and the resulting query lands in someone else's logs before it lands in someone else's index.

A local-first harness can do better. Public search engines like DuckDuckGo and Wikipedia expose endpoints that work without an account or an API key. A harness that aggregates those endpoints in-process keeps the query inside the user's network boundary. The vendor — whether Anthropic, OpenAI, or anyone else — never sees it.

The implementation is mostly plumbing: a Backend interface, two scrapers, an aggregator that runs them in parallel, a fetcher that pulls each result page, and an extractor that strips the navigation and ads. Wrap each result in a <source> tag so the model treats it as untrusted reference material. Done.

For privacy-conscious users, optional SOCKS5 proxy support routes every outbound call through Tor or Mullvad. Combined with the local-first design, the user's IP address never lands in DuckDuckGo's logs either.

What this is not

It is not a custom search index. It is not a ranking model. It is a thin coordinator over endpoints that already work. Future iterations can add SearXNG for users who self-host that excellent privacy proxy.
